posts.author: hi89
posts.body:
Hello! I'm a web developer with 5 years of experience.
I'm currently using RPG Maker MZ, and while I don't need to install plugins, I do want to make some customizations, so I've been researching various aspects.
I've concluded that to create plugins or make customizations, you need to understand how to use the classes defined in the
rmmz_*.js
files located in the
PROJECT_ROOT\js
directory.
Some of the usage can be inferred by reading the code, but to use them accurately, official documentation is necessary.
However, the only documentation I've found is
https://developer.rpgmakerweb.com/rpg-maker-mz/index.html
, and it's not enough. Are there any additional documents available?
For example, I need explanations about the
Scene_Title
class and how to use its properties and methods.
I hope I'm not expected to figure all this out on my own.

posts.author: ATT_Turan
posts.body:
Welcome!
hi89 said:
Some of the usage can be inferred by reading the code, but to use them accurately, official documentation is necessary.
Click to expand...
Why?
hi89 said:

Click to expand...
No.
hi89 said:
I hope I'm not expected to figure all this out on my own.
Click to expand...
You are. That's what everyone else who writes plugins that affect the UI has done.
I don't want to insult your knowledge or make presumptions about your skill level, but if you have 5 years of experience with JavaScript you should be able to understand the code and follow the path of function calls.
Trihan has a series of posts called Jump Into JavaScript:
MV - Jump into Javascript, a breakdown and explanation of the default js files in MV.
This is a companion series to Slip into Ruby (my teardown of the RPG Maker VX Ace default scripts) and aims to teach a bit of Javascript while explaining exactly how everything works under the hood of MV's .js files.  Part 1: https://rpgmaker.net/tutorials/1230/ (main.js, rpg_scenes.js...
forums.rpgmakerweb.com
They go through the core script files and describe in English what each function is doing - but, again, one would expect an experienced coder to be able to read that. And as far as I know, the articles are unfinished and don't provide any kind of more in-depth explanation of processes.
Do you have specific questions about the title screen? What are you trying to do?

posts.author: Mac15001900
posts.body:
Unfortunately that's it. MV does have community-made Typescript annotations which are rather helpful (including an overall description of what each class is for), but I'm not sure if something similar exists for MZ.
And while it doesn't cover UI,
here
is a useful resource for all event-related code.
hi89 said:
while I don't need to install plugins
Click to expand...
I highly recommend that you still do. They will save you some effort in making things yourself, but more importantly they're also a great learning opportunity for figuring out how to do various things in the engine. I assume JavaScript won't be a problem for you, but knowledge of what parts of the engine do what is still something that will probably require some effort to acquire.

Yeah, basically, you will have to read the code and understand it. If you are used to have reference guides or literal documentation....yeah, this software has never had that kind of guides or documentation as you would find for example in Java or even .NET...and even those are not great but at least they explain things. Also, don't expect plugins to have detailed information, even from those that you pay for, literally you can find better documentation of and old obscure database from the 70s than the code from RPG Maker MV or MZ...and MV had better documentation than MZ in my opinion, but still lacking.  But the code is not that complex, so if you have already experience with large software development, you shouldn't have too much trouble.
ATT_Turan said:

Click to expand...
You do have a point, but in general I would disagree, good software code base should have a relative basic description of what a particular object does, what the methods do, expect as parameters and the expected results. It's true that when you already have experience with coding, you might deduce things just by reading the code. I might be going off topic, but over the years and working with multiple coding languages, even some very obscure or almost going out of use, good documentation saves you hours of development. RPG Maker has rather good user documentation, but not, or almost nothing, code base documentation...and it seems to be a rather common issue on game engines, the code is not very well explained, and is expected that the developer reads thousands of lines of code before doing something...which makes the learning curve too steep.

I still really don't get what you're trying to get at here.
The correct comparison to Java and .NET languages is JavaScript. Every single JavaScript function and bit of syntax is thoroughly described and documented.
JavaScript reference - JavaScript | MDN
The JavaScript reference serves as a repository of facts about the JavaScript language. The entire language is described here in detail. As you write JavaScript code, you'll refer to these pages often (thus the title "JavaScript reference").
developer.mozilla.org
Understanding how this program works, which was written in JavaScript, is just as difficult or easy as understanding how a
program written in
Java or a .NET language works. All of these languages can have custom data types defined which will not exist in the language's documentation, and will certainly have their own functions which don't have any reference in the language's documentation.
This comparison you're bringing up is kind of like saying "I don't know who all the characters in A Game of Thrones are, but it's easy to understand the dictionary." They're two completely different things.

And yeah, it would be like, let me look at a Game of Thrones character dictionary to at least know which side each one is, a quick overview and where in the plot from a particular book we are with them, it helps since is a series with a lot of story and pages, often you get lost. If it were the Little Prince for example...that would be overkill but still welcomed.
So, to OP. MV had something like you were looking for on the F1 Contents section, but it didn't have everything you are looking for, so you have to eventually open up the code and look for what you need. MZ has an even more generalized version in the same F1 Contents section, less classes documented, only very high level clases, but still, you won't get anything from a particular window, or a particular screen, you'll get the Window super class or things like that. In that regard RPG Maker is very bad for documentation of the code side for developers who are used to work with standard documentation.
